shape.name: Shape E - Receptive Skills (Traditional)
shape.description: Traditional receptive skills lesson focusing on practicing listening or reading sub-skills.
shape.pedagogical_justification: Here the focus is not on language but on practicing receptive skills and helping learners process written and audio text. The overall aims might be: By the end of the lesson, learners will have practiced and developed the sub-skills of listening for gist and detailed comprehension. You should also include the context as part of the aim, e.g. ... in the context of a news report about smart glasses. The lesson opens with a listening entry ticket (a famous song gap-fill) that activates schema and pre-listening vocabulary.
shape.main_aim_format: By the end of the lesson, learners will have practiced and developed the sub-skills of [reading/listening] for [gist/detail/specific information] in the context of [topic].

example_lesson_plan.header:
Objective:
By the end of the lesson, learners will have practiced and developed the sub-skills of listening for gist and detailed comprehension in the context of a news report about smart glasses and privacy.
Teacher:
Ed Rush
Date:
17-08-26
Duration:
46 minutes
CEFR Level:
B1
Lesson Shape:
E (Receptive Skills - Listening)
Materials:
Worksheet, slideshow, BTN news video, song audio (Tom's Diner)
Assessment:
Entry ticket gap-fill, listening tasks, discussion observation
Skills:
Listening

stages.stage_aim: To activate schema and practice listening for key words
procedure: Show the Suzanne Vega picture. In pairs, students predict what the song is about. Use Opinion-Reason-Evidence.
Give the song facts (written 1982, used to test the MP3 format, 1990 remix became a hit).
Play the 44-second snippet once. Students answer the multiple-choice question about the song's meaning. Check.
Students open their worksheets. Play the whole song once. They complete the 24 lyric gaps.
Display the answer slides. Students swap and mark.

stages.stage_aim: To set the context for the main listening
procedure: Show the splash slide. Ask: What do you see? What might this be about? Let students speculate.
Advance to the title slide: Should smart glasses be allowed? Confirm the theme.
Ask: What are smart glasses? Do you know anyone with them?

stages.stage_aim: To listen for the main idea of the news report
procedure: Tell students to watch the video once without writing.
Play the BTN video (Meta Smart Glasses).
Students choose the main idea (A-D) on the worksheet. Check the answer (B).

stages.stage: Listening for detail and specific information
stages.stage_aim: To listen for specific information and identify true/false statements
procedure: Play the video again. Students complete the six detail sentences on the worksheet.
Check the detail answers.
Students complete the true/false section and correct the false ones. 4-minute timer.
Check the true/false answers (1 F, 2 T, 3 T, 4 T, 5 F).

stages.stage_aim: To use the listening content to form and defend an opinion
procedure: In groups, students discuss: Should smart glasses be banned?
Each student writes their opinion and three supporting ideas on the worksheet outline.
Groups share opinions, agree or disagree using the language table, and reach a conclusion. 5-minute timer.
Each group reports one conclusion to the class. Content feedback first, then language feedback.

stages.stage_aim: To consolidate the lesson and check understanding
procedure: Ask: What did you decide? Should smart glasses be allowed?
Elicit a few group conclusions.
Quick recap: Which listening words were new for you today?

metadata.topic: Smart glasses and privacy - listening and decision-making
materials: Worksheet: Smart Glasses - Listening & Discussion (entry ticket gap-fill, gist, details, true/false, discussion outline)
Video: BTN - Meta Smart Glasses news report (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=I1BzGOfh4L0)
Song: Tom's Diner by Suzanne Vega (entry ticket listening)
metadata.main_aim: By the end of the lesson, learners will have practiced and developed the sub-skills of listening for gist and detailed comprehension in the context of a news report about smart glasses and privacy.
metadata.subsidiary_aim: Learners will also have practiced listening to a song for key words (gap-fill) and will discuss and reach a conclusion on a privacy issue using opinion and agreement language.
answer_key: Snippet question: B - The quiet story of an ordinary moment. A woman sits in a diner and watches people come and go.

Gap-fill answers (24): 1. on, 2. the, 3. only, 4. out, 5. nice, 6. To, 7. her, 8. are, 9. them, 10. the, 11. died, 12. had, 13. looking, 14. and, 15. the, 16. does, 17. reflection, 18. up, 19. hair, 20. through, 21. the, 22. the, 23. began, 24. to.
The video is mainly about B: what smart glasses can do, and why some people worry about them.
1. Smart glasses have been around since the early twenty-tens.
2. Ray-Ban and Meta worked together in 2021.
3. The Kmart version costs $89 and sold out last week.
4. The glasses can respond to voice commands, play music, and make calls.
5. Some use AI to translate foreign languages instantly.
6. Filming in a bathroom, changeroom, or bedroom is illegal.
True or False - Correct the False Ones
1. False - Smart glasses first appeared in the early twenty-tens, not 2021.
2. True - The Kmart glasses sold out last week.
3. True - In Australia, filming people in public places is usually allowed.
4. True - You must ask permission before filming on private property.
5. False - Filming without knowledge is not necessarily against the law, but many people say it is not ethical.
